summary: Specifies how NAT devices should behave when handling ICMP, making them more predictable and compatible with the many applications whose traffic passes through them. It is a companion to other documents on NAT behavior requirements and is a best current practice.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5508 describes how traditional IPv4 NATs should handle ICMP messages. Its requirements help queries reach their replies and help error messages find the traffic they describe.

questions: how should a nat handle icmp
how long should a nat keep icmp query mappings
why does nat need to translate icmp errors
subtitle: Requirements for how traditional IPv4 NATs handle ICMP queries, errors and other messages.

tldr.problem: Network Address Translators (NATs) handle Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) traffic in different ways, making applications that rely on queries or error reports less predictable.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5508 sets requirements for ICMP query mappings and timeouts, validation and translation of ICMP errors, hairpinning, outbound-flow rejection and other ICMP message types.
tldr.outcome: The Best Current Practice applies to traditional IPv4 NATs and is updated by RFC 7857.

today: RFC 5508 is Best Current Practice 148, published in April 2009. It has been updated by RFC 7857.

sections.title: Scope: Traditional IPv4 NATs
sections.content:
RFC 5508 specifies behavior for traditional Network Address Translators (NATs) handling the Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP). Its goal is to reduce unpredictable differences between NATs and improve compatibility with applications that cross them.

The requirements apply to Basic NAT and Network Address Port Translation (NAPT) in an IPv4 environment. The RFC covers ICMP Query messages and ICMP Error messages, with some guidance for other ICMP messages. General firewall behavior and application behavior are outside its scope.

Local administrative policy can override some behavior. For example, an administrator may prohibit ICMP errors or applications based on ICMP queries.
sections.plainLanguage: This document sets behavior for traditional IPv4 NATs when they handle ICMP. Local policy can still block some ICMP traffic.

sections.title: Three Categories of ICMP Messages
sections.content:
The RFC separates ICMP messages into three groups because each gives a NAT different information for identifying traffic.

  • ICMP Query messages have an Identifier, called the Query Id. The Query Id identifies a query session in a way similar to a TCP or UDP port.
  • ICMP Error messages contain part of the original IP datagram that caused the error. The RFC calls it the embedded packet.
  • Non-QueryError messages do not fit either category. Router Discovery messages are an example because they lack a Query Id and are not ICMP errors.

A NAT session links a session's private-realm representation with its public-realm representation after translation.
sections.plainLanguage: Queries have an identifier, errors quote the packet that caused them, and other ICMP messages fit neither group. The NAT uses these different clues to find the right traffic.

sections.title: Mapping ICMP Queries and Keeping State
sections.content:
Unless local policy overrides it, a NAT must allow an ICMP Query started by a private host and its associated response. A NAPT device translates the IP header and also translates the Query Id and ICMP checksum.

A NAT should use an external-host-independent mapping for Query Ids. If the same private host reuses a Query Id for a query to another external host, the NAT should reuse the same public mapping. The RFC sets this as a SHOULD because existing applications do not require it, though future applications might.

An ICMP Query session timer must not expire in less than 60 seconds, and the timer is recommended to be configurable. The RFC explains that a shorter timeout could release state before a reply arrives, while a longer one keeps NAT resources occupied.
sections.plainLanguage: The NAT keeps a mapping so a query's reply can return to the private host. It must keep that mapping for at least 60 seconds.

sections.title: Validating and Translating ICMP Errors
sections.content:
An ICMP Error contains a fragment of the packet that triggered it. The NAT uses that embedded packet to find the related NAT session. If the ICMP checksum is invalid, or the embedded IP checksum is invalid, the NAT should silently drop the error. If the embedded IP packet has options, the NAT must skip them to locate the transport header. The NAT should not validate the embedded transport checksum, since the error often contains only part of that transport data.

If no active mapping matches the embedded packet, the NAT should silently drop the ICMP Error. If a mapping exists, the NAT translates the embedded IP and transport headers back to their original form and leaves the ICMP type and code unchanged. It also translates the outer IP header according to whether the error came from the external or private realm.

When processing an error related to an ICMP Query or response, the NAT must not refresh or delete the associated NAT session. This prevents a spoofed error from changing that session's state.
sections.plainLanguage: The NAT checks the error message and uses its quoted packet to find the right mapping. It translates the addresses, but the error itself must not extend or remove the related query session.

sections.title: Hairpinning and Rejected Outbound Traffic
sections.content:
Hairpinning occurs when traffic between private hosts passes through the NAT using its public address. Basic NAT must support hairpinned ICMP Query sessions. Basic NAT and NAPT must support hairpinned ICMP Error messages and translate the outer destination address to match the translated source address of the embedded packet.

If a NAT cannot create a session for a new flow because of resource limits or administrative restrictions, it should send the sender an ICMP Destination Unreachable message with code 13, Communication administratively prohibited, and drop the original packet. The RFC says this is primarily for future use and strongly discourages taking resources away from existing sessions instead.
sections.plainLanguage: Private hosts must be able to use the NAT's public address to reach one another through it. If the NAT cannot create a new session, it should report the problem instead of taking another session's resources.

sections.title: Which ICMP Messages a NAT Handles
sections.content:
Unless a policy under REQ-9 overrides it, REQ-10 says a NAT must support Destination Unreachable, Time Exceeded and Echo Request/Reply messages. A NAT may support Redirect, Timestamp, Source Route, Address Mask, Parameter Problem and Router Advertisement or Solicitation messages. It should not support Source Quench or Information Request/Reply messages.

A NAT must honor the Don't Fragment bit. If it cannot forward a packet without fragmentation, it must send a Packet Too Big ICMP message (type 3, code 4) with the next-hop MTU and drop the packet. It must also forward Packet Too Big messages it receives and generate Time Exceeded when a packet's TTL expires.

For Non-QueryError messages, the RFC gives no further handling rules: a NAT may drop them or handle them appropriately.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC requires support for common error and echo messages, while allowing some less-used types to be optional. A NAT must report when a packet cannot be forwarded without fragmentation.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says it introduces no new security concerns and that some requirements reduce known ICMP risks. Checksum validation helps filter malformed errors, and dropping errors without matching sessions prevents them from reaching an unrelated host. These checks do not by themselves protect end hosts from all attacks.

REQ-6 prevents an ICMP Error from changing the state of the related query session. The RFC also notes that an administrator may choose not to send the rejected-flow error because it could confirm to an attacker that a restriction or resource limit was reached.

Blocking ICMP at network boundaries can break path MTU discovery, ping and traceroute. The RFC says such blocking is not recommended.
sections.plainLanguage: Checksum checks and session matching can filter some bogus errors, but they do not prevent every attack. Blocking ICMP can also disrupt path MTU discovery and familiar diagnostic applications.
